Integration
Blueprint

How Wise's existing product experience maps to Lean's account-to-account rails for the UAE market - funding, recurring money movement, and payouts on local open-banking infrastructure.

Prepared by
Aliaa Moharram
Market
UAE
Vertical
Remittance

Wise can bring its funding, recurring-money, and payout experiences to the UAE on Lean's account-to-account rails, replacing card and correspondent fees with open-banking pricing. This blueprint maps each Wise flow to the Lean product that powers it, sizes the value at stake, and lays out the path to go-live.

01

Pain points & opportunities

Wise runs on local rails in its other markets - direct debit, local schemes, and card networks. Bringing the same product experience to the UAE means moving funding, recurring pulls, and payouts onto local account-to-account infrastructure. These are the remittance pain points Lean addresses, split by business and technical impact.

Business impact

Pain point / opportunityHow Lean solves itAdvantage
Card fees erode thin margins on top-ups and collections. Lean Pay by Bank for bank-to-bank top-ups and collections as a lower-cost alternative to cards. Lower take-rates, improved unit economics, and more pricing flexibility per corridor.
Volatile rates, spreads, and correspondent fees vary by corridor, squeezing competitiveness. Reduce card dependence and improve settlement predictability. Higher, more stable margins per corridor through lower acceptance costs.

Technical & operational

Pain point / opportunityHow Lean solves itAdvantage
Multiple payment methods and payout rails increase integration and ops complexity. A single integration for Pay by Bank and Payouts, with normalized references and clear statuses across banks. Faster time-to-market and leaner operations, with less engineering effort and support load.
Bank variability and inconsistent references make for a non-standard experience across banks and corridors. Consistent payment references across banks, handling different bank formats. More predictable ops and faster exception handling across markets.
Heavy AML / KYC expectations, especially source-of-funds and beneficiary ownership checks, add operational burden. Name verification on pay-ins, in development at Lean and targeted for Q4, will support payer screening and ownership checks. Reduced manual document collection, better compliance posture, smoother UX.
02

The remittance journey, end to end

Told as one money lifecycle: a UAE customer funds their Wise balance, automates recurring money movement and pays out locally. The journeys split along two lines: the direction of funds (money in vs money out) and the payment permission (the customer authenticates each payment vs one standing agreement), because each combination is a different Lean product, a different customer experience, and a different piece of the build. Each step below is an existing Wise experience (shown in-app) mapped to the Lean product that powers it in the UAE.

Wallet top-upScheduled remittanceSavings automationCorridor payoutBill paymentPay a request
Journey 1 Funding a Wise balance

Top up from your bank

Wise feature
Add money, then pay from a connected bank account.
The need
Pull AED from the customer's own bank to fund their Wise balance.
Lean powers it
One-Time PaymentsRecurring PaymentsA One-Time Payment for one-off top-ups; a Payment Agreement for repeat top-ups (authorise once, charge on demand).
Journey 2 Paying a payment link

Pay a request by bank

Wise feature
Wise payment links: a Wise user who receives one pays it from their Wise balance or by manual bank transfer.
The need
Let the payer pay from their Wise balance or with Pay by Bank, straight from their bank account.
Lean powers it
One-Time PaymentsRecurring PaymentsA One-Time Payment for a single payment, or a charge under the payer’s existing Payment Agreement if they’ve already connected their bank account, the same as Journey 1.
Journey 3 Recurring funding

Money on autopilot

Wise feature
Recurring, scheduled top-ups, for example automating savings into a Jar on a set cadence.
The need
Keep the Wise balance funded on schedule, without asking the customer each time.
Lean powers it
Recurring PaymentsOne Payment Agreement, many scheduled charges. Ahead of each scheduled run, Wise creates a charge under the agreement to top up the balance. What happens next is handled inside Wise: an internal move (a savings Jar) stays put, while an outbound send goes out as a payout (Journey 4).
Journey 4 Payouts & bill payments

Pay out locally

Wise feature
Sending to a recipient's UAE bank account.
The need
Pay out to any UAE bank account.
Lean powers it
PayoutsPayouts for the transfer, initiated server-side.

03

Launch Plan

How the integration is delivered: the Lean products involved, what ships in each phase, the APIs behind it, and the effort to build.

Lean products

In scope

One-Time Payments

A single Pay by Bank payment, represented by a Charge, that funds the Wise balance directly from the customer's bank.

In scope

Recurring Payments

A Payment Agreement gives reusable permission to charge: on demand, on a schedule, or in instalments. The engine behind repeat top-ups and scheduled transfers.

Future

Payouts

Outbound transfers to UAE bank accounts, initiated server-side. An open decision on Wise's side.

Future

Data

Account insights for income-based decisions, such as salary verification for lending and credit limit increases.

Future

Cards

Cards and further payment methods as values on the same Charge integration, with no re-integration.

Delivery phases

Phase 0

Setup

  • Developer portal: sandbox app token, credentials, redirect URLs, webhooks and a test user
  • Authentication: an access token for every API call, then your Settlement Account
  • Webhooks: signed payment events, handled once and in any order
Phase 1

Funding journey

  • Account-to-account pay-in (One-Time + Recurring Payments)
Phase 2

Verified pay-ins

  • Screen the actual payer: Wise-supplied name and the bank-returned account holder name on every new account connection
  • Name match at payment initiation: in development at Lean, targeted for Q4
Future phases

Payouts, Data and Cards

  • Payouts to UAE accounts: an open decision on Wise's side
  • Data: account insights for income-based decisions, in discovery
  • Cards: further payment methods on the same Charge integration; Lean's cards product is in build, KSA first, UAE to follow

Phase 0 · Implementation guide
Developer portal setup
Set up your application on the Lean dev portal in Sandbox: app token, Open Finance, client secret, redirect URLs, webhooks and a test user. Production comes once Lean upgrades you.
How it works
Sandbox to production
Integration checklist
  1. Create an account on the Lean dev portal.
  2. Create your application. The portal starts in Sandbox mode: do every step below in Sandbox until Lean upgrades you to production.
  3. Copy the application ID the portal generates: your sandbox app tokenYour application ID from the dev portal, sent as client_id. Sandbox and production each have their own.. Share it with Lean in the box after these Sandbox steps.
  4. Ask Lean Support to enable Open Finance on your application.
  5. In Development, Integration settings, generate your client secret and store it on your backend. Retrieving it again invalidates the existing one.
  6. In Settings, add your redirect URLs. The host is enough, for example https://app.yourcompany.com: Lean only sends customers back to URLs set up here.
  7. In Settings, add the purpose statement and the benefit statement customers see when they authorise a payment, in English and Arabic.
  8. In Development, Webhooks, add a webhookAn HTTPS POST Lean sends to your backend when a payment resource changes, for example charge.captured. with the HTTPS endpoint where your backend receives events, for example https://api.yourcompany.com/webhooks/lean.
  9. Select these webhook events, then save. In the event list they’re under Other.
    Charge eventsOne-Time and Recurring Payments4
    charge.createdA new Charge is created.
    charge.capturedThe Charge is captured.
    charge.declinedThe payment was declined.
    charge.discardedAuthentication wasn’t completed in time.
    Agreement eventsRecurring Payments7
    agreement.activatedThe Agreement is authorised.
    agreement.suspendedThe Agreement is paused.
    agreement.resumedThe Agreement is ACTIVE again.
    agreement.declinedThe Agreement was rejected.
    agreement.discardedThe customer didn’t complete authentication.
    agreement.fulfilledThe Agreement reached its completion conditions.
    agreement.revokedThe Agreement is permanently withdrawn.
    Instrument eventsthe bank accounts customers pay from2
    instrument.createdA new Payment Instrument is created.
    instrument.updatedAn instrument’s stored details change.
    Optional: refundsonly once you refund payments4
    charge.refundedThe full captured amount is refunded.
    refund.pendingA Refund is waiting to complete.
    refund.succeededThe Refund completed.
    refund.failedThe Refund failed.
  10. In Development, Integration settings, copy your webhook signing secretThe secret Lean signs each webhook with (the lean-signature header). It’s in Development, Integration settings.. It’s separate from your client secret: your backend uses it to verify every webhook (see Webhooks).
  11. In Development, open the test-user management section and create a Sandbox test user: set its details and the scenarios you need, then save. You’ll use its details to authenticate in Sandbox. Test users are separate from the Lean Customers your API calls create.
Production

Once Lean upgrades you to production. These steps aren’t counted in Phase 0 progress.

  1. Switch the dev portal to production mode.
  2. Copy the newly generated production application ID (app tokenYour application ID from the dev portal, sent as client_id. Sandbox and production each have their own.).
  3. In Integration settings, generate your production client secret. Sandbox and production credentials are separate, so your sandbox secret won’t work in production.
  4. Set up production webhooks: the production endpoint, its signing secret and the same events (see the Webhooks guide).
  5. Start calling production endpoints with the production credentials.

Phase 0 · Implementation guide
Authentication and API basics
Get an access token for every API call, then make your first one: creating your Settlement Account.
Before you start
  • Your app token and client secret from Developer portal setup.
  • Your business details: trade licence number, registered address, and the bank account that receives your funds.
How it works
Getting an access token
Keep in mind
  • Keep your app token and client secret on your backend only, never in a client-side app or source control.
  • Send an Idempotency-KeyA unique key sent with a create request. Retrying with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a duplicate. with every create request. If a request times out, retry with the same key; never reuse a key with a different body.
  • Lean is the source of payment state: a customer returning to your app means their authentication finished, not that the payment succeeded. Use the resource’s status or its webhook.
Integration checklist
  1. Configure your backend with the Sandbox addresses: the API at https://sandbox.leantech.me and the token endpoint on auth.sandbox.leantech.me. You’ll switch both when Lean upgrades you to production.
  2. Generate an access token from your backend with POST /oauth2/token on auth.sandbox.leantech.me: your app token as client_id, your client secret, grant_type client_credentials and scope api for backend calls (customer.<customer_id> for customer-scoped calls).
  3. Send the token on every API call as Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  4. Create your Settlement AccountThe bank account where the funds you collect through Lean are transferred. You create it with the API (a Payment Destination with no customer_id) and send its id as settlement_account_id.: POST /payments/v1/destinations with your business and bank details, and no customer_id, so the account belongs to your application. The fields are in the reference below; don’t use special characters in any of them, as banks may reject the details. Store the id Lean returns in your backend configuration as settlement_account_id.
Production

Once Lean upgrades you to production. These steps aren’t counted in Phase 0 progress.

  1. Create your production Settlement Account with the same call on https://api.leantech.me, and use its id as settlement_account_id in production.
Reference: Settlement Account request
FieldWhat to send
bank_identifierYour bank’s Lean identifier, for example NBF_OF_UAE.
nameThe account holder’s name, as the bank has it.
ibanThe account’s IBAN.
display_nameA friendly name for the account.
statusCONFIRMED.
address, cityThe address registered with the bank, and its city. Keep it short, with no special characters.
countryThe three-letter country code: ARE.
bank_typeRETAIL, SME or CORPORATE.
customer_idLeave it out, so the account belongs to your application.

The API reference also lists account_number, swift_code and government_identifier (TRADE_LICENSE_NUMBER and its value). Add them if Lean asks for them.

Example request (sample values: replace them with yours):

{
  "bank_identifier": "YOUR_BANK_IDENTIFIER",
  "name": "YOUR COMPANY LLC",
  "iban": "AE070331234567890123456",
  "display_name": "Settlement Account",
  "status": "CONFIRMED",
  "address": "Office 101 Business Bay",
  "country": "ARE",
  "city": "Dubai",
  "bank_type": "SME"
}

POST /oauth2/tokenPOST /payments/v1/destinations

Phase 0 · Implementation guide
Webhooks
Receive payment and instrument events on your backend: verify them, acknowledge them fast, and process them safely.
Before you start
  • Your webhook endpoint, its events and its signing secret, from Developer portal setup.
How it works
How a webhook is delivered
Handling duplicate deliveries
Integration checklist
  1. Store the webhook signing secretThe secret Lean signs each webhook with (the lean-signature header). It’s in Development, Integration settings. from Developer portal setup on your backend only: never in a client-side app or source control.
  2. Make your endpoint publicly reachable over HTTPS, accepting POST requests and returning HTTP 200 within 10 seconds.
  3. Verify the lean-signature header on every request: HMAC-SHA512 of the raw request body with your signing secret, formatted sha512=<hash>. Reject invalid signatures.
  4. Acknowledge fast: verify, store or enqueue the event, return HTTP 200, then process it asynchronously.
  5. Deduplicate on event_id: Lean delivers at least once, so skip IDs you’ve already processed.
  6. Don’t rely on order: identify the resource from the payload and fetch its current state when you need to decide something, with GET /v4/payment-charges/{charge_id} or GET /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}.
Production

Once Lean upgrades you to production. These steps aren’t counted in Phase 0 progress.

  1. Configure webhooks separately for production: the production endpoint, its signing secret and the same events.
Reference: webhook fields
FieldWhat it is
event_idUnique ID for the event. Use it to detect duplicate deliveries.
typeThe event, for example charge.captured.
messageA readable description of the event.
timestampWhen the event happened, in UTC.
payloadThe resource the event is about. Its contents depend on the event: some events carry the full resource, others its ID and new status.
{
  "event_id": "evt_6Lp3Rd9Km",
  "type": "charge.captured",
  "message": "The charge has been captured.",
  "timestamp": "2026-07-17T10:05:44.612Z",
  "payload": {
    "id": "chg_oneoff75Qk",
    "status": "CAPTURED",
    "capture_id": "cap_8dF2Qm",
    "amount": { "value": "75.00", "currency": "AED" }
  }
}
Reference: signature and code example
PropertyValue
Headerlean-signature
AlgorithmHMAC-SHA512
Formatsha512=<hash>
Signed contentThe raw HTTP request body
SecretYour webhook signing secret

Example in Node.js. Calculate the signature over the raw body: parsing and re-serialising the JSON changes the bytes and breaks verification.

const crypto = require("crypto");

// rawBody: the request body exactly as received (a Buffer), before any JSON parsing.
function isFromLean(rawBody, signatureHeader, signingSecret) {
  if (!signatureHeader || !signingSecret) return false;
  const expected = "sha512=" + crypto.createHmac("sha512", signingSecret).update(rawBody).digest("hex");
  const a = Buffer.from(signatureHeader, "utf8");
  const b = Buffer.from(expected, "utf8");
  return a.length === b.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b);
}

// Express: keep the raw body on the webhook route.
app.post("/webhooks/lean", express.raw({ type: "application/json" }), async (req, res) => {
  if (!isFromLean(req.body, req.get("lean-signature"), process.env.LEAN_WEBHOOK_SECRET)) return res.sendStatus(401);
  const event = JSON.parse(req.body.toString("utf8"));
  await saveIfNew(event); // your durable store or queue, keyed on event.event_id
  res.sendStatus(200);    // acknowledge first, process asynchronously
});
Reference: retry schedule

Lean delivers at least once, so an event can arrive more than once. A delivery fails if your endpoint doesn’t return HTTP 200 within 10 seconds. Failed deliveries are retried on this schedule:

RetryAfter
11 minute
22 minutes
35 minutes
410 minutes
560 minutes
6180 minutes
Reference: payment events

Events can arrive out of order: charge.captured can arrive before charge.created. Treat each one as a notice that the resource changed.

Charge events (standalone Charges and Charges under an Agreement)
EventWhen it’s sentWhat to do
charge.createdA new Charge is created.Record it against your order or transaction.
charge.capturedThe Charge is captured.Mark the payment successful. Settlement is requested; the funds may not have reached your Settlement Account yet.
charge.declinedThe payment was declined.Read decline_reason. Terminal: create a new Charge to retry.
charge.discardedAuthentication wasn’t completed in the allowed window.Close the attempt. Terminal: create a new Charge to retry.
Agreement events
EventWhen it’s sentWhat to do
agreement.activatedThe Agreement is authorised.Enable charging. Only an ACTIVE Agreement can be charged.
agreement.suspendedThe Agreement is paused.Stop initiating new Charges.
agreement.resumedThe Agreement is ACTIVE again.Resume charging where appropriate.
agreement.declinedThe Agreement was rejected.Read decline_reason; offer a new authorisation if appropriate.
agreement.discardedThe customer didn’t complete authentication.Create a new Agreement if needed.
agreement.fulfilledThe Agreement reached its completion conditions.Stop creating Charges and mark it completed.
agreement.revokedThe Agreement is permanently withdrawn.Stop charging under it.
Instrument events
EventWhen it’s sentWhat to do
instrument.createdA new Payment Instrument is created: when you create one, or when Lean captures one while processing a payment (for example, when the customer selects the account to pay with).Store it against the customer. The payload is the complete instrument, in the same shape as Fetch Payment Instrument, so no follow-up fetch is needed.
instrument.updatedAn instrument’s stored details change.Replace your stored copy with the payload (the complete instrument after the change) rather than merging fields.

Delivery is at least once and unordered: dedupe on event_id. Example instrument.created (sample values):

{
  "event_id": "evt_4Tn8Vb2Xw",
  "type": "instrument.created",
  "message": "The instrument has been created.",
  "timestamp": "2026-07-17T10:01:12.284Z",
  "payload": {
    "id": "ins_bank7Yt2Qp",
    "type": "BANK_ACCOUNT",
    "customer_id": "3f8e2c4a-9b1d-4e6f-8a2c-5d7b9e1f3a60",
    "details": {
      "iban": "AE070331234567890123456",
      "swift_code": "ADCBAEAAXXX",
      "holder_name": "Sample Customer"
    },
    "display_name": "AE**** **** **** 0123",
    "fingerprint": "fpr_ka9f2ubmqk5d5wcz"
  }
}
Refund events (optional, once you refund payments)
EventWhen it’s sentWhat to do
refund.pendingA Refund is waiting to complete.Mark the refund as processing.
refund.succeededThe Refund completed. Each partial refund sends its own.Update the refunded amount.
refund.failedThe Refund failed.Read decline_reason; decide whether to try again.
charge.refundedThe full captured amount is refunded.Mark the payment fully refunded.
If you run into these
  • Your network restricts inbound traffic: allowlist Lean’s UAE webhook senders. IP addresses and hostnames
  • A delivery failed or an event wasn’t processed: check the delivery history and resend it from the dev portal. Monitor and resend deliveries
  • You need to change your endpoint or rotate the signing secret. Manage webhooks
  • You receive an event type you don’t recognise: acknowledge it after verifying and storing it, and record it for investigation. Handle unknown events

Phase 1 · Implementation guide
One-Time Payments
Accept a single Pay by Bank payment. Each payment is a ChargeA Charge is a single payment. Every payment is a Charge, whether it stands alone or is made under an Agreement., tracked from creation through the customer’s authentication to its outcome.
Before you start
  • Phase 0 done: an access token and your settlement_account_id (Authentication), and webhooks (Webhooks). You’ll test the whole flow in the End-to-end test.
How it works
The payment lifecycle
A one-time payment
Keep in mind
  • Use the Charge’s state to determine the payment outcome, rather than assuming that the customer returning from authentication means the payment succeeded. The customer has 10 minutes to authenticate; after that the Charge is discarded.
Integration checklist
  1. Create a Charge from your backend: POST /v4/payment-charges with an Idempotency-KeyA unique key sent with a create request. Retrying with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a duplicate., payment_method PAY_BY_BANK, the amount in AED, your settlement_account_id, your references (charge_merchant_reference, authorization_merchant_reference) and authentication_overrides with a return_url and fail_return_url on a host you added in Developer portal setup.
  2. For a customer’s first payment, create the CustomerThe person paying. Lean creates the Customer with their first Charge or Agreement and returns a customer_id to reuse. in the same request with a customer block; store the customer_id Lean returns. For their later payments, send customer_id instead.
  3. Store the Charge id against your order before sending the customer anywhere. You’ll use it to fetch the Charge and match webhooks.
  4. Send the customer to the REDIRECT method’s details.url from available_authentication_methods. They choose their bank and the account to pay from, and Lean creates a Payment InstrumentA Payment Instrument is a funding source, created once and then referenced by its id from Charges and Agreements. For Pay by Bank it’s a bank account: IBAN, SWIFT code and holder name. Lean creates one when the customer selects the account to pay with. for that account and sends instrument.created. On the web, redirect the browser. In a mobile app, open it in a WebView: close the WebView on your own return URL, keep Lean-hosted URLs inside it, and hand any other URL to the operating system so the bank app opens.
  5. When the customer returns, check the outcome with GET /v4/payment-charges/{charge_id} and show it from the Charge’s state:
    • CAPTURED: show success. Settlement is requested; the funds may not have arrived yet.
    • DECLINED: show failure, using decline_reason.
    • PENDING_PROVIDER_CONFIRMATION: show a pending state and listen for webhooks (charge.captured or charge.declined), then update the customer. This happens in under 2% of payments, but your integration still needs to handle it.
    PENDING_CUSTOMER_AUTHENTICATION means authentication isn’t finished yet; DISCARDED means it wasn’t completed in time. Declined and discarded are final: create a new Charge to retry.
  6. Handle charge.captured, charge.declined and charge.discarded: they matter most when the customer never comes back to your app. Store the instrument from instrument.created, and replace it when instrument.updated arrives.
Reference: Charge statuses
StatusWhat it meansWhat to do
PENDING_CUSTOMER_AUTHENTICATIONThe customer still needs to authenticate.Wait for the customer or a webhook.
PENDING_PROVIDER_CONFIRMATIONWaiting for final confirmation from the provider. Happens in under 2% of payments.Show a pending state and listen for webhooks (charge.captured or charge.declined), then update the customer. Build for it even though it’s rare.
CAPTUREDThe payment succeeded and settlement is requested.Confirm the payment.
DECLINEDThe payment was declined.Read decline_reason; allow a new payment.
DISCARDEDNot completed within the 10-minute window.Create a new Charge to retry.
Endpoints
POST /v4/payment-chargesGET /v4/payment-charges/{charge_id}

Phase 1 · Implementation guide
Recurring Payments
Collect repeat payments under one Payment AgreementA Payment Agreement is a customer’s permission to be charged over time. It doesn’t move money itself: each payment under it is a Charge.: the customer authenticates once, and each payment under it is its own ChargeA Charge is a single payment. Every payment is a Charge, whether it stands alone or is made under an Agreement..
Before you start
  • Phase 0 done: an access token, your settlement_account_id and webhooks. The One-Time Payments flow, since every Charge under an Agreement behaves the same way. You’ll test the whole flow in the End-to-end test.
How it works
Recurring payments on demand
Keep in mind
  • Each Charge under an Agreement behaves like a one-time payment, with its own status and charge.* events, including the scheduled Charges Lean creates. Track the Agreement’s status separately from each Charge’s.
Integration checklist
  1. Choose how payments are created: on demand (your app creates each Charge), a recurring schedule (plan.type RECURRING) or instalments (EXPLICIT).
  2. Create the Agreement: POST /v4/payment-agreements with an Idempotency-KeyA unique key sent with a create request. Retrying with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a duplicate., payment_method PAY_BY_BANK, currency AED, a customer block (or customer_id for a returning customer) and limits that match what the customer agrees to. Add a plan for scheduled payments, and optionally settlement_accounts or an initial_charge.
  3. Store the Agreement id against the customer, then send them to the REDIRECT method’s details.url, the same way as a one-time payment. The customer chooses the account to pay from, and Lean creates a Payment InstrumentA Payment Instrument is a funding source, created once and then referenced by its id from Charges and Agreements. For Pay by Bank it’s a bank account: IBAN, SWIFT code and holder name. Lean creates one when the customer selects the account to pay with. for it and sends instrument.created.
  4. Confirm activation with agreement.activated or GET /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}. Only charge an ACTIVE Agreement; DECLINED and DISCARDED are final, so start a new Agreement to retry.
  5. Charge on demand: POST /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}/payment-charges with an Idempotency-Key, the amount, authorization_merchant_reference and payment_descriptor. If the response includes available_authentication_methods, send the customer through it. Show each Charge’s outcome from its state, the same way as a one-time payment: CAPTURED shows success, DECLINED shows failure, and PENDING_PROVIDER_CONFIRMATION shows pending until a webhook arrives.
  6. Manage the Agreement: pause with POST /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}/pauses (SUSPENDED), resume with /resumptions (ACTIVE) and revoke with /revocations (REVOKED, permanent).
  7. Handle the Agreement events: agreement.activated, agreement.suspended, agreement.resumed, agreement.declined, agreement.discarded, agreement.fulfilled and agreement.revoked. Track the Agreement’s status separately from each Charge’s.
Reference: limits
LimitWhat it controls
per_charge_max_amountMaximum amount of one Charge.
agreement_max_total_amountMaximum total charged under the Agreement.
agreement_max_charges_countMaximum number of Charges.
expiration_dateDate after which the Agreement can’t be used.

If you omit a limit, the payment provider may apply its own: read the Agreement response for the limits in effect.

Reference: Agreement statuses
StatusMeaningCan you charge it?
PENDING_CUSTOMER_AUTHENTICATIONAuthentication is outstanding.No
ACTIVEAuthorised and chargeable.Yes, within its limits
SUSPENDEDTemporarily paused.No
FULFILLEDReached its completion conditions.No (final)
REVOKEDPermission withdrawn.No (final)
DECLINEDDeclined by the customer or provider.No (final)
DISCARDEDAuthentication wasn’t completed.No (final)
Reference: schedules
PlanHow it works
RECURRINGA fixed amount at a fixed frequency: amount, start_date, recurrence.unit (DAY, WEEK, MONTH), recurrence.interval, and an end_condition (NEVER, AFTER_COUNT or ON_DATE). Fixed once created: changing it needs a new Agreement.
EXPLICITInstalments on set dates, each with a unique reference, a charge_on date and an amount. The Agreement reaches FULFILLED after the last one.
Endpoints
POST /v4/payment-agreementsGET /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}POST /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}/payment-chargesPOST /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}/pausesPOST /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}/resumptionsPOST /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}/revocations

Phase 1 · Implementation guide
Consent Management Interface (CMI)
Build Lean’s CMI natively in your app: users see their Pay by Bank agreements and payments, and can revoke an agreement. Lean signs it off at three gates before Pay by Bank goes live in production.
Before you start
  • Lean’s Native CMI Implementation Requirements, and the CMI screens in Figma (see Design reference). The native CMI replaces the Link SDK’s manageConsents() function.
  • One-Time and Recurring Payments built: the CMI reads the AgreementsA Payment Agreement is a customer’s permission to be charged over time. It doesn’t move money itself: each payment under it is a Charge. and ChargesA Charge is a single payment. Every payment is a Charge, whether it stands alone or is made under an Agreement. they create.
How it works
Sign-off: three gates before go-live
Revocation: one API call, only after Confirm
Keep in mind
  • Server-to-server only: the Lean token and client secret stay on your backend, never in the app. The app talks only to your backend.
  • Customer scope is your check: Lean’s reads are scoped to your application, not the customer. Check customer_id on every read, including IDs sent from the app, and never return records that fail it.
  • The list endpoints can’t filter by customer_id, so don’t build a user’s CMI from them: store every agreement_id and one-time charge_id against the user, and read them back by ID.
  • Phase 1 builds Payments only. Design the Data screens for sign-off, but keep the Data tab hidden from users until Lean issues the Data requirements.
1. Gate 1 · Design review
  1. Sections 2 and 4Design every CMI screen and state
    As Lean, we can review every CMI screen and state in your designs before you build.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Covers the Payments list, payment consent details (Active, Revoked, Expired), Terms, Payment history, payment details, and the revocation confirmation, success and failure screens (sections 5 to 8).
    • Covers the loading, empty, no-results and error states (section 9, STA-01 to STA-07).
    • Uses Lean’s consent design system in light mode (Reference: design system), not your own design system.
    • Matches the frames in Lean’s Figma.
  2. Sections 3.8, 5.3 and 6Design the Data screens
    As Lean, we can review the Data screens now, so they’re ready when Data ships.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Covers the Data list, and data consent details in Active, Expired and Revoked, with the copy in sections 5.3 and 6.
    • Tapping a Data tile opens that consent’s details (DAT-01), and the list has no Connect another account footer (DAT-02).
    • Cancel permission on an Active data consent starts the data revocation flow (DAT-05). No Pause button unless you build pause / resume (DAT-03), and no footer action on Expired or Revoked (DAT-04).
    • Permission labels use the three labels in the WISE CMI DESIGNS / active data consent frame, in that order.
    • Not built or shown to users in Phase 1. When Data goes live, Lean confirms the default tab and whether an empty tab is hidden or shows its empty state (GEN-05).
  3. GEN-06Design Arabic, right to left
    As an Arabic-speaking user, I can use the CMI in Arabic.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Screens are mirrored, text is right-aligned and directional icons are flipped.
    • Required at launch.
  4. Section 2, Gate 1Get the design review signed off
    As your team, we have Lean’s sign-off on the designs before we build.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Figma (or equivalent) for every screen and state in sections 5 to 9 is shared with Lean.
    • Lean has checked it against its designs and the acceptance criteria in section 10, and signed it off.
2. Build · Data and APIs
  1. Section 3.2Store consent IDs against the user
    As your backend, I keep every agreement and one-time charge ID against the user who created it, so the CMI only reads that user’s records.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Every agreement_id from POST /v4/payment-agreements is stored against the user.
    • Every one-time charge_id from POST /v4/payment-charges is stored against the user.
    • The CMI is never built from the agreement or charge list endpoints: they can’t filter by customer_id, and no filter is planned.
  2. Sections 3.2 and 3.3Read consents and payments by ID
    As your backend, I fetch each user’s consents and payments from Lean by ID.
    Acceptance criteria
    • An access token from POST /oauth2/token with a form body of client_id, client_secret, grant_type=client_credentials and scope=api (L1), sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>. Auth host: https://auth.sandbox.leantech.me in Sandbox, https://auth.leantech.me in production.
    • API base: https://sandbox.leantech.me in Sandbox, https://api2.leantech.me in production.
    • Agreements by ID (L2); one-time charges by ID (L4).
    • Charges per agreement, following next_cursor until has_more is false, page_size up to 100 (L3).
    • The payer’s Payment InstrumentA Payment Instrument is a funding source, created once and then referenced by its id from Charges and Agreements. For Pay by Bank it’s a bank account: IBAN, SWIFT code and holder name. Lean creates one when the customer selects the account to pay with. (L5), and the bank name and logo from GET /banks/v1, matched on swift_code and cached (L6). Lean provides the bank names and logos.
  3. Section 3.2Return only the user’s own records
    As a user, I only ever see my own consents and payments.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Every read checks that customer_id is the signed-in user’s Lean customer, including IDs sent from the app.
    • Records that fail the check are never returned.
  4. PAY-02, section 3.4Show the right records
    As a user, I see my Pay by Bank permissions and payments, without pending or failed ones.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Payments tab: PAY_BY_BANK agreements only. ACTIVE under Active; REVOKED and FULFILLED under Expired (LPG has no EXPIRED status; FULFILLED shows as Expired).
    • Never shown: PENDING_CUSTOMER_AUTHENTICATION, PENDING_PROVIDER_CONFIRMATION, DECLINED, DISCARDED; SUSPENDED unless you build pause / resume (tell Lean first, and Lean designs the Paused state).
    • Payment history: the charges under those agreements plus stored one-time PAY_BY_BANK charges, hiding PENDING_CUSTOMER_AUTHENTICATION, DISCARDED, REFUNDED and VOIDED.
    • Agreements are sorted by created_at, newest first; Payment history merges all charges, newest first.
  5. Sections 3.5 and 3.6Map every field from Lean’s data
    As a user, every value I see comes from Lean’s data.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Each field is mapped as in Reference: field mapping, including the purpose labels.
    • Total paid to date is the sum of CAPTURED charge amounts (LPG exposes no consumption totals).
    • A row is hidden when its source field is absent, including limit rows: no empty or “null” values, and no Figma placeholder text (Label, Text, Badge, {{reference}}).
  6. Section 3.7Format amounts, dates and names
    As a user, amounts, dates, IBANs and names look consistent everywhere.
    Acceptance criteria
    • AED amounts use the UAE Dirham symbol (16 × 16) before the number, except Payment history rows and the payment details title, which use the “AED” prefix as designed.
    • Amounts are formatted from Lean’s decimal strings without floating point, with a comma thousands separator: 2 decimal places for totals and charges, and limits without decimals when whole.
    • Dates are DD/MM/YY on list subtitles and Data screens, and D MMMM YYYY on agreement details, Payment history and payment details. Lean’s timestamps are UTC: show them in the device time zone. “Last payment {when}” reads today, yesterday or D MMMM YYYY.
    • IBANs are masked as **** + last 4, except “Your IBAN”, shown in full and grouped in 4s.
    • {TPP} and {MerchantName} are your company name, as a static string.
  7. Section 3.2Keep consents up to date
    As a user, I see the latest state of my consents, including revocations at my bank.
    Acceptance criteria
    • The CMI re-fetches on every open and after every revocation.
    • On agreement.activated, agreement.suspended, agreement.resumed, agreement.fulfilled, agreement.revoked, charge.captured, charge.declined and charge.discarded, the resource is re-fetched.
    • Duplicate and out-of-order webhooks are handled. agreement.revoked carries a source of MERCHANT, CUSTOMER or PROVIDER; PROVIDER means it was revoked at the user’s bank.
3. Build · Screens
  1. GEN-01 to GEN-04Open the CMI
    As a user, I can open my Open Finance connected accounts and switch between Payments and Payment history.
    Acceptance criteria
    • The CMI opens as a bottom sheet over the scrim on your Connected accounts page, and Close dismisses it from every screen.
    • The tab selector sits at x24, 76 pt below the sheet top, in a 39 pt high tap area with radius 14 (Tab selector style). It opens a picker with Data, Payments and Payment history, in that order, and the selected option becomes its label.
    • It opens on Payments, and the Data option is hidden in Phase 1.
  2. PAY-01, section 5.2See and search my payment permissions
    As a user, I can see my payment permissions grouped into Active and Expired, and search them by bank name.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Header: Close only, the company avatar, the title “Open Finance connected accounts”, and the description “You have given us payment permissions for these accounts. Tap on each option to view, update or cancel your permission.” with a “Read more” link (URL from Lean). Drop “update” unless you build update.
    • A “Search consents” field filters both groups by bank name, case-insensitive, as I type; a group with no consents hides its heading (STA-03).
    • Active tile: bank avatar and name, “Last payment {when}”, “Expires on {DD/MM/YY}”, and the total paid on the right with a chevron.
    • Expired tile: “Permission cancelled {DD/MM/YY}” when revoked, or “Expired on {DD/MM/YY}”, with a chevron and no amount column. The optional line can show “Total paid {Dirham} {amount}”; account type has no LPG field, so it’s hidden (Q20).
    • Tapping a tile opens its details. No Connect another account control is shown.
  3. PAY-03, PAY-07, section 7.1View a permission’s details
    As a user, I can see the full details of a payment permission.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Bank name with its status badge, and “To make instant payments with Wise you gave us your consent to your {Bank name} accounts since {DD/MM/YY}.”
    • Total paid to date, consent ID, where the money was sent (masked IBAN) and purpose.
    • Payment rules: start and expiry dates and each limit, each hidden when absent.
    • The “Permission to check balance” and “Share account details” tiles with their copy, and a Terms tile.
    • Last payment made, its amount, the from account (bank name and masked IBAN), and a Payment history link filtered to this agreement (PAY-07).
    • Values stay on one line, right-aligned, and truncate with an ellipsis (PAY-03).
  4. PAY-04, PAY-05Cancel permission only when active
    As a user, I can cancel an active permission; expired and revoked ones are shown for reference only.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Cancel permission is shown on Active agreements only.
    • It is never shown on Revoked or Expired, even though the revoked Figma frame shows it.
    • Tapping it starts the revocation flow.
  5. PAY-06Read the terms
    As a user, I can read the End user agreement and Privacy Policy.
    Acceptance criteria
    • The Terms screen lists both, and each opens in an in-app browser.
    • URLs are supplied by Lean (open item Q13).
  6. HIS-01, HIS-02See my payment history
    As a user, I can see the payments made from my connected accounts, newest first.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Header: Close only, the company avatar, the title “Payment history” and “A record of the payments made from your connected accounts.”
    • Each row shows the bank avatar, amount, date, status badge (Successful, Pending, Rejected) and a chevron.
    • Successful, Pending and Rejected rows open payment details.
    • More payments load as I scroll (HIS-02); SHOULD show a spinner row at the end while the next page loads (STA-02).
  7. HIS-03, HIS-04View a payment’s details
    As a user, I can see a payment’s details and copy its references.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Title “AED {amount}”, “Paid to {recipient name}” (the static company name), and the amount, status and date.
    • The title amount and the Amount row show the same value.
    • Paid to with masked IBAN, paid from, and my IBAN in full.
    • Payment frequency (“On demand” or “One-time”), consent ID (hidden for one-time payments) and description.
    • The copy icon copies the full value (HIS-03 MUST), and SHOULD confirm with your standard toast.
  8. STA-01 to STA-07Loading, empty and error states
    As a user, I can always tell whether the CMI is loading, empty or has failed.
    Acceptance criteria
    • SHOULD: skeleton rows while loading (Skeleton_Description-List), with the header shown straight away (STA-01).
    • An empty tab shows its title and description, hides search, and shows an empty message; no search results hides both groups and shows a no-results message (copy reviewed by Lean).
    • A failed fetch keeps the header, shows an inline error with Retry, and never shows stale data as current.
    • When a bank logo fails, its initials show on the bank’s main_color.
  9. STA-08Accessible for everyone
    As a user of assistive technology, I can use every CMI screen.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Every tap target is at least 44 × 44 pt.
    • Badges, icons and avatar pairs have screen-reader labels, for example “Status: Active”.
4. Build · Revocation
  1. REV-01Confirm before cancelling
    As a user, I’m asked to confirm before a permission is cancelled.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Cancel permission opens the confirmation screen, with no API call yet.
    • Cancel or Back returns to the consent details unchanged; Close dismisses the CMI.
    • The revocation call is made only when I tap Confirm.
  2. Sections 8.2 to 8.4Confirmation, success and failure screens
    As a user, I understand what cancelling means, and whether it worked.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Confirmation: title “The impact to your service”; “You are about to disconnect your {LFI} accounts, so we will no longer be able to initiate payments on demand with {MerchantName}”; the “What are the implications?” block; the payer account (L5) under “The accounts you shared access to”; the Privacy Notice footnote; and “Are you sure you want to disconnect this account from our service?” with Confirm (Al Tareq primary) and Cancel (Al Tareq outline).
    • Payments use the payment-specific success screen and implications copy from Lean’s CMI revocation flow Figma, which Lean is to link (open item Q11).
    • Success: check-circled icon on its ripple, “Disconnection successful”, its body copy, a Close button and the Privacy Notice footnote.
    • Failure: exclamation-triangle icon, “Disconnection failed” and “We couldn’t disconnect your accounts from {LFI} at this moment. Please try again later.”
  3. REV-02Revoke once, safely
    As your backend, I revoke an agreement exactly once per confirmation.
    Acceptance criteria
    • On Confirm, both buttons are disabled and Confirm shows a spinner.
    • The call is POST /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}/revocations with a new Idempotency-KeyA unique key sent with a create request. Retrying with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a duplicate. per confirmation and {"reason":"END_USER_REQUESTED"}.
    • Double taps and back-and-retry make no duplicate calls; retrying the same confirmation reuses the same key.
  4. Sections 3.3 and 8.1Handle the result
    As a user, I’m shown the right result.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Success on 200, or on 409 when re-fetching the agreement shows REVOKED (for example, already revoked at the bank).
    • Failure on 400, 404, 5xx, or no response within 30 seconds, with the consent unchanged.
  5. REV-03Return to an up-to-date list
    As a user, I return to an up-to-date list after cancelling.
    Acceptance criteria
    • There’s no way back from success or failure to the confirmation screen.
    • Close on success returns to the re-fetched list, with the agreement under Expired and “Permission cancelled {today}”.
    • Close on failure returns to the consent details, unchanged.
5. Gate 2 · Sandbox build review
  1. Section 2, Gate 2Demo the build in Sandbox
    As Lean, we can see the build working against Sandbox.
    Acceptance criteria
    • The demo runs against sandbox.leantech.me with agreements in every displayed status (ACTIVE, REVOKED, FULFILLED) and charges in every displayed status.
    • Screen recordings show the agreement revocation flow end to end, including the failure state.
    • Data screens are reviewed as designs only.
  2. Section 10Visual and copy parity
    As Lean, we can confirm the build matches the designs.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Every screen in sections 5 to 8 matches its Figma frame 1:1: layout, spacing, radii, colours, type and icons.
    • All copy matches sections 5 to 8 word for word, including punctuation and capitalisation.
    • The Al Tareq gradient, button variants and status badges match the design system, and no placeholder text appears anywhere.
  3. Section 10Data and scope
    As Lean, we can confirm the CMI shows the right data.
    Acceptance criteria
    • The Payments tab shows PAY_BY_BANK agreements only; Payment history shows their charges plus one-time PAY_BY_BANK charges.
    • Every Payments field matches the LPG response for at least one agreement and charge in each displayed status; null fields hide their row; amounts, dates and IBANs follow section 3.7.
    • View and revoke work end to end. Pending, DECLINED and DISCARDED agreements never appear, the Data tab is hidden, and no Connect another account control is shown.
    • Update, pause / resume and reconfirm controls appear only if you build them, and pass Lean review.
    • An agreement’s status reflects a revocation at the bank after agreement.revoked or on next open.
  4. Section 10Revocation and security
    As Lean, we can confirm revocation works and users’ data is protected.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Revocation completes end to end in Sandbox, and the agreement moves to Expired with the Revoked badge.
    • No API call before Confirm, no duplicate calls on double tap, and the failure screen shows on an error or timeout. Cancel and Back leave the consent unchanged.
    • The Lean token is never in the app bundle or the app’s network traffic.
    • A user can only see and revoke consents for their own customer_id.
6. Gate 3 · Production readiness
  1. Section 2, Gate 3Production sign-off
    As your team, we can take Pay by Bank live once Lean has signed off production.
    Acceptance criteria
    • The production build is identical to the signed-off sandbox build.
    • Lean has confirmed in writing. This is a precondition for Pay by Bank going live in production with real users, not only for releasing the CMI screens.
  2. Section 2, Gate 3Changes after go-live
    As Lean, we review any CMI change before it’s released.
    Acceptance criteria
    • Any change to CMI screens, copy or data mapping gets a fresh Lean review before release.
Source: this checklist and its references are built from Lean’s Native CMI Implementation Requirements (UAE OF). for the full wording.
Optional (MAY): if you build any of these, Lean reviews and signs them off
  • Update, pause / resume or reconfirm of consents. If you build reconfirm, you set the threshold and copy for the “Expires in {X} days, tap to reconfirm” line.
  • Dark mode.
Reference: API calls
#CallUsed forNotes
L1POST /oauth2/tokenAccess tokenscope=api. Production auth host: https://auth.leantech.me.
L2GET /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}Payments list, agreement detailsOne call per stored agreement_id.
L3GET /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}/payment-chargesPayment history, total paid, last paymentCursor pagination, newest first: follow next_cursor until has_more is false; page_size up to 100.
L4GET /v4/payment-charges/{charge_id}Payment details; one-time charges in Payment historyStored charge_id.
L5GET /v4/payment-instruments/{instrument_id}Payer account: details.iban, details.holder_name, details.swift_codeinstrument_id from L2, L3 or L4.
L6GET /banks/v1Bank name and logoMatch on swift_code; cache. Lean provides bank names and logos.
L7POST /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}/revocationsRevoke an agreementHeader Idempotency-Key (required); body {"reason":"END_USER_REQUESTED"}. 200: revoked. 409: re-fetch L2; REVOKED means success. 400, 404, 5xx or timeout: failure screen.

API base: https://sandbox.leantech.me in Sandbox and https://api2.leantech.me in production. Auth: https://auth.sandbox.leantech.me and https://auth.leantech.me. Header Authorization: Bearer <token>.

AreaSpec (from the requirements, section 4)

Phase 1 · Implementation guide
End-to-end test in Sandbox
Run the whole integration against the Sandbox, in order: environment, a one-time payment, a recurring payment, webhooks and failure cases. When every step passes, you’re ready for production.
Before you start
  • Phase 0 done: dev portal setup (including a test user), authentication (including your Settlement Account) and webhooks.
  • One-Time and Recurring Payments built from their guides.
How it works
The end-to-end run in Sandbox
1. Environment
  1. Point your backend at the Sandbox: API base https://sandbox.leantech.me, token endpoint on auth.sandbox.leantech.me, and your sandbox app token and client secret. Sandbox and production credentials are separate.
  2. Get an access token and make one API call with it. Then call without a token and confirm you get 401.
  3. Confirm your backend uses the sandbox settlement_account_id from Developer portal setup, and that your Sandbox test user (Developer portal setup, step 12) is ready.
2. A one-time payment
  1. From your real checkout code, create an AED 75 Pay by Bank ChargeA Charge is a single payment. Every payment is a Charge, whether it stands alone or is made under an Agreement. with an Idempotency-Key, your settlement_account_id, your references, a customer block and your return_url and fail_return_url.
  2. Check the response: status PENDING_CUSTOMER_AUTHENTICATION, a REDIRECT method with details.url and a customer_id. Confirm your app stored the Charge id and the customer_id before redirecting.
  3. Open details.url on the web and in your app’s WebView, choose an account, and complete authentication with your test user’s details. Confirm the customer lands back on your return_url.
  4. Confirm the outcome from Lean, not the return: GET /v4/payment-charges/{charge_id} shows CAPTURED; your endpoint received charge.created, instrument.created and charge.captured, verified lean-signature and returned 200 within 10 seconds; your order shows as paid.
  5. Make a second payment for the same customer, sending customer_id instead of customer. Confirm both Charges belong to the same Lean Customer.
3. A recurring payment
  1. Create an on-demand AgreementA Payment Agreement is a customer’s permission to be charged over time. It doesn’t move money itself: each payment under it is a Charge. with limits, open its details.url and authorise it with your test user. Confirm ACTIVE through agreement.activated and GET /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}.
  2. Charge it with POST /v4/payment-agreements/{agreement_id}/payment-charges. Confirm the Charge belongs to the Agreement, has the right amount and currency, follows the usual lifecycle, and sends charge.captured.
  3. Try a Charge above per_charge_max_amount: it’s rejected, and your app handles it.
  4. If you use schedules: create a RECURRING Agreement and check its amount, frequency and end condition, or an EXPLICIT one and check its dates, amounts and references.
  5. Pause the Agreement (SUSPENDED, agreement.suspended) and confirm a new Charge is rejected. Resume it (ACTIVE, agreement.resumed). Revoke it (REVOKED, agreement.revoked) and confirm it can’t be charged again. If your limits or plan can complete, run one to FULFILLED (agreement.fulfilled).
4. Webhooks
  1. In the dev portal’s webhook delivery history, confirm every event from the runs above arrived and your endpoint returned 200.
  2. Resend one of those events from the dev portal and confirm your backend skips it as a duplicate (event_id).
  3. Send your endpoint a request with a wrong lean-signature and confirm it’s rejected.
  4. Process an event out of order, for example charge.captured before charge.created, and confirm your records still end up correct by fetching the current state.
  5. Take your endpoint offline, make a payment, then bring it back. Confirm Lean’s retry arrives (the first after 1 minute) and is processed once.
5. Failure cases
  1. Decline a payment with a test-user scenario: the Charge becomes DECLINED, you show decline_reason, and the customer can start a new Charge.
  2. Abandon authentication and wait out the 10 minutes: charge.discarded arrives and the Charge is DISCARDED.
  3. Complete authentication but don’t follow the return to your app: your backend still records the outcome from the webhook or the API.
  4. Decline or abandon an Agreement: it becomes DECLINED or DISCARDED, and your app offers a new one.
  5. Retry a create request with the same Idempotency-KeyA unique key sent with a create request. Retrying with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a duplicate.: you get the original Charge back. Reuse the key with a different body: it’s rejected.
  6. Send invalid parameters (validation error), an invalid token (401) and a call you don’t have permission for (403), and confirm your app handles each.
6. Ready for production
  1. Go through Lean’s go-live checklist: authentication works; the Settlement Account is configured; Pay by Bank is tested; successful and unsuccessful outcomes are handled; Charges and Agreements belong to the right customers; create requests are idempotent; webhook signatures are verified; duplicate and out-of-order webhooks are handled; outcomes come from resource statuses; production credentials and webhooks are ready.
Going live

After the production steps in Developer portal setup and Webhooks. These aren’t counted in progress.

  1. Change the API base URL to https://api.leantech.me and use your production credentials. Don’t reuse Sandbox credentials or test users in production.
  2. Confirm your production Settlement Account and that Pay by Bank is enabled for your production application.
  3. Complete Lean’s go-live validation before processing live customer payments.

Payouts
Server-to-server outbound transfers to UAE bank accounts. No customer-facing screen.
Before you start
  • Authenticate with the Lean API.
  • Fund the payout account.
  • Your webhook endpoint receiving payment_source.beneficiary.created, payment_intent.created, payment.created and payment.updated.
How it works
Integration checklist
  1. Create the payout destination: POST /payouts/v1/payment/destinations with the beneficiary’s details. Wait for payment_source.beneficiary.created before making a payout to it.
  2. Create the payout: POST /payouts/v1/payment with an idempotency key so retries never double-pay.
  3. Track each payout: payment_intent.created arrives for each payment in the payout; payment.created carries its first status (AWAITING_AUTHORIZATION or FAILED); then payment.updated carries the bank’s status (AUTHORIZATION_FAILED, ACCEPTED_BY_BANK, PENDING_WITH_BANK or FAILED). ACCEPTED_BY_BANK isn’t a completed payment until the funds are reconciled. Read the final outcome from post_initiation_status (PROCESSED or REJECTED), also available from GET /payouts/v1/{payoutId}. Handle failed payouts and retries explicitly.
  4. Test in Sandbox: a successful payout, a failed payout and retry, and a duplicate payment.created delivery.
Endpoints
POST /payouts/v1/payment/destinationsPOST /payouts/v1/payment
